d.title: It is written like a blocking call, and the process ended in between
d.caption: `interrupt()` **behaves like a blocking call from the node's point of view** — it returns the human's answer. **What happens in between is that the process ended, the state was written to a checkpoint, and a later invocation resumed from it.** So the illusion is complete at the level of the source and the mechanism underneath is suspend-and-restore, which is why §03's re-execution behaviour is surprising: the code reads as if nothing was interrupted.

d.title: The node body ran twice for one logical execution
d.caption: **The node is re-executed from its first statement**, and this time `interrupt()` returns the resume value instead of pausing. So **anything before the interrupt runs twice** — the measurement shows `side effect 1` on the first pass and `side effect 2` on the resume. **The pattern is to make the interrupt the first thing the node does and put the action in a separate node after it.** A genuinely non-obvious constraint, and the whole reason approval gates are their own node rather than a check inside the acting node.

d.title: This one refuses, and 9.4's accepted — which is the better behaviour
d.caption: `interrupt()` **without a checkpointer raises**: pausing with nowhere to store the paused state cannot mean anything, **so refusing is correct.** Worth noticing because **9.4's `thread_id` with no checkpointer is accepted and ignored** — the same missing dependency, one failure loud and one silent. The loud one is the better design, and the comparison is the clearest argument in the module for why the silent one is a trap rather than a convenience.

nodes.label: The loud one is the better design

d.title: Approve, reject and edit are three values, not three features
d.caption: **The node inspects whatever it was handed and branches on it**, so the gate needs no knowledge of which outcomes exist — which is why **9.8's approval gate is a single reusable node.** And it is the argument for **designing the resume payload as a small schema rather than a bare string**: `{'action': 'edit', 'value': ...}` carries a correction, and `'approve'` carries nothing, and a gate written for the second cannot be extended to the first without changing both ends.

d.title: update_state is an update like any other, so every reducer applies
d.caption: Paused before a refund of 9999.00, `update_state` corrected the amount to 50.00 and the resumed run executed the corrected one. **Notice `'amount corrected'` was appended to the trace rather than replacing it** — `update_state()` is **an update like any other**, so 8.3's reducers apply in full. Which means editing state while paused cannot *remove* anything from a reduced key: to replace rather than append you need 8.3's id-based replacement, not a state edit.

d.title: They differ only when a node has several successors
d.caption: For a two-node graph `interrupt_after=["prepare"]` and `interrupt_before=["execute"]` are **the same pause.** They diverge when a node has several successors: **after prepare is one pause; before each successor is several.** And for approval, **`interrupt_before` on the acting node is the right choice, because what you are gating is the action** — which also **stays correct when someone later adds another path into that node**, where the `after` version would not gate the new path at all.

nodes.label: And a new path into it is still gated

d.title: Most approvals should depend on the request
d.caption: **A static breakpoint pauses every time.** The dynamic gate asks only when the condition says to: **a 50.00 refund is auto-approved and a 500.00 one waits for a human**, who can approve or deny. Which is the shape production approval actually needs — refunds over a threshold, writes to production, anything irreversible — because **approving everything is a workflow nobody sustains and approving nothing is not a gate.**

d.title: Static for debugging, dynamic for anything where asking is itself logic
d.caption: Five differences, and the last is the one that decides it in a codebase: **a static breakpoint breaks on a node rename** — it is configuration referring to a name, which 8.5 established is public structure — while a dynamic gate breaks only if you change the node it lives in. **Use static for debugging and for a blanket *never act unattended* policy. Use dynamic for anything where the decision to ask is itself logic**, which is most production approval.

cells.text: carries a payload and a response
breaks only if you change the node

d.title: Five checkpoints, and the state before the decision is already there
d.caption: A three-node run leaves **five checkpoints, each with a step number, the next node and the state at that point.** Reading an earlier one answers *"what did the state look like before the decision"* **without re-running anything** — which is the debugging use on its own, and **the state is already there: you paid for it by checkpointing.** Which is §04's argument in advance: this is not a feature to enable, it is a thing you have already bought.

d.title: The counterfactual is answerable by replaying, not reasoning
d.caption: The original had `n=10` at step 1. `update_state(n=100)` **returns a new checkpoint config rather than mutating the old one**, so re-running from there gives **`add_ten -> 110`, `final n=110`** — and **the original branch is still there to compare against.** Which is what the name *time travel* is pointing at: *"what would it have done if n had been 100 there"* is **answered by replaying rather than by reasoning about the code.**

d.title: Not an additional feature with an additional cost
d.caption: 9.4's cost is **a checkpoint per superstep, each holding the whole internal state.** Time travel **is not an additional feature with an additional cost — it is the thing checkpointing already bought.** So **the question is whether you use it, not whether to enable it**; and the sharp version of that: **a team paying for per-superstep persistence and still debugging by adding log lines and re-running is paying twice.**

nodes.label: So time travel costs nothing more
The question is whether you use it
Log lines plus a re-run is paying twice

d.title: Forking re-executes nodes, with a wider blast radius than 9.7's
d.caption: **Everything 9.7 said about re-execution applies again**, and further: a fork replays whole nodes, side effects included. **The idempotency-key case is the one where the right answer is genuinely ambiguous** — replaying with the old key makes the downstream call a no-op, **which is correct for recovery and wrong for a counterfactual where you want the action to happen differently.** So: **time travel is safe on a graph of pure computation and model calls, and needs care the moment a node acts on the world** — 9.7's conclusion, reached from the other side.
